{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOQ3jMp88AAAABXrMKQA", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4Bm6oxzhBPZQ4", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4Bm6ox", "number": 5, "title": "Improve TSL Node Editor UI/UX with a reference-driven workspace redesign", "body": "## Problem

TSL Node Editor has gained substantial functionality, including node graph editing, a live WebGPU preview, code/glTF export, custom functions, history, groups, and local storage. However, the interface has grown incrementally rather than around a consistent workspace design.

Currently, `src/App.tsx` places Node Palette, Overlay, History, Layout and Storage in a single vertical sidebar, while the node graph and the 3D preview occupy an overlaid viewport and the code viewer opens as an overlay. Node controls and connection pins can be dense and small. This makes it harder to see the graph and its visual output at the same time, discover frequent actions, and understand the selected node.

We should improve visual hierarchy, layout and everyday workflows **without sacrificing existing functionality**. Prioritize desktop editing first; keep narrower viewports usable.

## Expected outcome

Create a cohesive, modern, usable web-based material/node editor with:
- A clearly organized workspace for node graph, live 3D preview, and optional code/glTF output.
- A focused node/asset palette, easily discovered global actions, and contextual node/property inspection.
- Readable node cards, controls, pins, selection/focus/error states, and consistent spacing/typography.
- Efficient pan/zoom/navigation and a useful responsive layout.
- Preserved material preview, existing editor actions, and import/export behavior.

Use the following as **interaction/layout references**, not as visual assets to copy:
- [PlayCanvas Shader Editor](https://playcanvas.com/) — simultaneous graph, preview and inspector workflows.
- [NodeToy](https://nodetoy.co/) — approachable visual shader creation, discoverability.
- [Spline](https://spline.design/) — hierarchy, clean three-dimensional design-tool interface.
- [Figma](https://www.figma.com/) — contextual inspector and canvas toolbars.
- [React Flow examples](https://reactflow.dev/examples) — pan/zoom, fit-view, minimap and interaction patterns.
- [Blender Shader Editor](https://www.blender.org/), [Unreal Material Editor](https://www.unrealengine.com/), [Unity Shader Graph](https://unity.com/) — established node editing behavior and grouping.

## Proposed approach

### 1. Evaluate layout directions first

Document **2–3 concrete desktop layouts** before committing to the implementation. Compare at least:
1. Split workspace: left node palette, central graph, right dock combining 3D preview and contextual inspector.
2. Flexible graph-first workspace: docked/resizable preview, collapsible palette/inspector, code in a bottom/side panel.
3. A compact/tabbed alternative for smaller screens or limited width.

Compare each direction for simultaneous graph/preview visibility, discoverability, graph canvas area, implementation risk, and narrow-screen behavior. Select and document one primary direction (and its compact adaptation) using those criteria; do not stall on subjective approval unless truly necessary.

### 2. Apply the chosen layout

- [ ] Reorganize global commands (Undo/Redo, Auto Layout, Group/Ungroup, storage/project actions, export and view controls) into clear, discoverable menus/toolbars instead of an undifferentiated long sidebar.
- [ ] Keep node discovery/search prominent; group node and asset-related tools meaningfully, with clear empty states.
- [ ] Make graph editing and live 3D preview independently understandable and practical to see during editing; give code/material/app/glTF output a clear dock/tab or equivalent workflow.
- [ ] Add a contextual inspector for selected-node details where it improves usability, while retaining commonly adjusted values directly in node cards where useful.
- [ ] Apply a restrained, consistent dark visual system: semantic text/spacing/type scale, consistent action hierarchy, distinct node/card states, readable labels and contrast, and meaningful feedback/error states.
- [ ] Improve connection pin visibility and hit areas, selection/focus affordances, and graph navigation. Provide clearly available fit-to-graph and zoom controls; consider a minimap where helpful rather than mandating it.
- [ ] Keep the experience usable at narrower widths by collapsing/docking panels as needed; avoid making graph/node interaction unusable via CSS position resets.
- [ ] Preserve the existing editing model, saved graphs/slots, keyboard and pointer operations, undo/redo, grouping/functions, geometry and textures (including KTX2), WebGPU preview, and TSL/material/app/glTF/GLB export. No data format migration unless absolutely necessary.
- [ ] Keep implementation focused; modularize components/styles where it materially reduces risk, but avoid unrelated rendering/serialization or backend rewrites.

## Pre-merge acceptance criteria

- [ ] A checked-in short design comparison shows 2–3 layout alternatives, references, trade-offs, selected direction and a compact-screen adaptation.
- [ ] The implemented desktop workspace provides clear graph and 3D preview access concurrently, with discoverable node search, common commands, contextual editing and code/export views.
- [ ] Controls, labels, pins and focus/selection/error states are consistently legible and operable; icon-only actions have accessible names; keyboard focus is visible.
- [ ] Graph pan, zoom, selection, connection, group/function editing and relevant layout controls work after the reorganization; no pointer-event interception regressions from new docks/overlays.
- [ ] Existing storage save/load, Undo/Redo, WebGPU preview, glTF/GLB import/export (including `THREE_materials_tsl` Draft v2.0), and ordinary TSL output continue to work. Existing saved projects remain readable.
- [ ] Reasonable desktop and narrow-width viewport smoke checks document what was exercised; no panels cover all necessary editor controls or make the graph unusable.
- [ ] `npm ci`, `npm run build`, `npm run lint` and `npm run check:tsl` pass; run applicable existing browser checks when the environment supports them and explicitly report any skipped checks with reasons.
- [ ] Update README/docs or in-app help for materially changed command locations or workflows.

## Optional validation

- Side-by-side screenshots of the existing and redesigned workspaces for a small, medium and large node graph.
- WebGPU material visual verification on a physical GPU; lightweight user testing of node discovery and edit/export tasks.

## Required post-merge verification

Verify that GitHub Pages successfully publishes the new UI, and smoke-check the deployed editor's graph, preview and export controls. Keep this pending until deployment actually occurs.
